questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.stem: My oldest sister[[ Diana]] teaches chemistry at a high school.
questions.explanation: A person has only one oldest sister, so the name is unnecessary and needs commas on both sides. NO CHANGE drops both commas, and the single-comma choices leave the aside open on one end.

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.stem: The chemist[[, Rosalind Franklin,]] worked on the structure of DNA.
questions.explanation: 'The chemist' could name many people, so the name is necessary and takes no commas. The comma versions wrongly treat an essential name as removable.

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.stem: Because the elevator was broken[[ we]] climbed six flights of stairs.
questions.explanation: An introductory dependent clause is set off from the main clause with a comma, so ', we' is correct. NO CHANGE runs the clause into the main sentence, '; we' puts a semicolon after a clause that cannot stand alone, and ', we,' wrongly splits the subject from its verb.

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.stem: After the storm passed[[, we]] walked down to inspect the flooded dock.
questions.explanation: An introductory clause is set off from the main clause with a comma. Dropping the comma runs the clause into the subject, a semicolon needs a full clause before it, and the trailing comma misplaces the break.

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.stem: The novelist[[ Jane Austen]] published her first book anonymously.
questions.explanation: 'The novelist' fits many people, so the name is necessary and takes no commas. The comma versions wrongly set off an essential name as if it were removable.

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.stem: The tallest building in Chicago[[ the Willis Tower]] draws tourists year-round.
questions.explanation: Only one building can be the tallest in Chicago, so the name is unnecessary and needs a pair of commas. NO CHANGE uses none, and the single-comma options leave the aside half-open.

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.stem: My coworker[[, Priya,]] offered to cover my shift on Friday.
questions.explanation: 'My coworker' could be any of several people, so the name is necessary and takes no commas. The comma versions incorrectly treat an essential name as removable.

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.stem: The committee reviewed the budget[[, and]] approved the new hires before lunch.
questions.explanation: 'Reviewed' and 'approved' share the subject 'committee,' so no comma belongs before 'and' in this compound predicate. NO CHANGE inserts an unnecessary comma, ' and,' places a comma after the conjunction, and '; and' puts a semicolon before a phrase that cannot stand alone.

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.stem: Marcus's tent[[ a hand-me-down from his uncle]] survived the windstorm intact.
questions.explanation: The phrase describing the tent is extra information, so it needs commas on both sides. NO CHANGE uses none, and each single-comma choice leaves the appositive unbalanced or splits the subject from its verb.

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.stem: We waited in a cold[[ cramped]] room for nearly an hour.
questions.explanation: 'Cold' and 'cramped' are coordinate adjectives, since 'cold and cramped' and 'cramped, cold' both work, so a comma goes between them. No comma belongs between the second adjective and the noun, ruling out the paired and trailing-comma options.

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.stem: She inherited an antique[[, oak]] desk from her grandmother.
questions.explanation: 'Antique' and 'oak' are cumulative adjectives, since 'oak antique desk' and 'antique and oak desk' both fail, so no comma belongs between them. Each comma option wrongly splits the adjectives or separates an adjective from the noun.

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.stem: The book on the top shelf[[, however,]] belongs to the library, not to me.
questions.explanation: As an interrupting transition, 'however' is unnecessary information and needs commas on both sides. The no-comma choice drops both commas, and the single-comma choices drop one side and leave the aside unbalanced.

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?

questions.explanation: 'Quiet' and 'determined' are coordinate adjectives, since 'quiet and determined' and 'determined, quiet' both work, so a comma separates them. Removing it joins the adjectives wrongly, and the other options drop a comma between adjectives or add one before the noun.

questions.questionText: Which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable?
questions.stem: The waiter brought our food quickly[[ but]] he forgot to refill our drinks.
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses joined by 'but' need a comma before the conjunction. NO CHANGE omits that comma, ' but,' puts the comma after the conjunction instead, and ', but,' adds a second comma that splits the conjunction from its clause.
